A script is a sequence of steps with a name. The CIP cycle. The line purge.
The changeover to product B. Every plant has a handful of procedures it runs
exactly the same way every time, and the day somebody copies one into a
fourth automation and fixes a step in only three of them is the day it bites
you. So you write it once, give it a name, and everything that needs it calls
it by that name: an operator from the Scripts screen, a rule with a
`call_script` step, an agent with `run_script`, anything at all through
`POST /api/services/script/turn_on`.

A script speaks the automation language, runs on the same sequence runner a rule's actions do,
and every write it makes goes through the one write gate. No side door. It
never had one to begin with.

## What one looks like

```json
{
  "id": "cip_cycle",
  "name": "CIP cycle",
  "description": "Caustic wash, rinse, done. Tank must be empty.",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "minutes", "label": "Wash time", "type": "number", "min": 5, "max": 60, "step": 5, "unit": "min", "required": true},
    {"name": "circuit", "type": "select", "options": ["tank_1", "tank_2"], "default": "tank_1"}
  ],
  "sequence": [
    {"type": "condition", "params": {"expression": "float(states['sensor.cip_tank_level']) < 5"}},
    {"type": "call_service", "params": {"entityId": "switch.cip_pump", "service": "switch.turn_on"}},
    {"type": "delay", "params": {"seconds": 5}},
    {"type": "wait", "params": {"expression": "float(states['sensor.cip_return_temp']) > 70", "timeoutSec": 900}},
    {"type": "log_event", "params": {"message": "CIP on {{ vars.circuit }} for {{ vars.minutes }} minutes"}},
    {"type": "call_service", "params": {"entityId": "switch.cip_pump", "service": "switch.turn_off"}}
  ],
  "mode": "skip",
  "maxRuntimeSec": 1800
}
```

- **`id`** is lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a
  letter. It is also its entity's object id, so this one is `script.cip_cycle`,
  and it never changes.
- **`fields`** are what a run takes. Same typed inputs everywhere in HotLoop
  (`model.Field`): `number` with `min`, `max`, `step` and `unit`, `text` with
  `max_length` and `pattern`, `boolean`, `select` with `options`, `entity`
  with the `domain`s it takes, `duration` (seconds, or `90s`, `1h30m`),
  `alarm` and `tag`. Each can be `required` or have a `default`, and a default
  its own field would refuse is refused when you save. A step reads a field as
  `vars.<name>`.
- **`sequence`** is the automation language, the whole of it: `call_service`,
  `write_tag`, `condition`, `wait`, `stop`, `call_script`, `set_variable`,
  `delay`, `log_event` and the rest. [AUTOMATIONS.md](/iot/automations/) has
  every step.
- **`mode`** and **`maxRuntimeSec`** are below.

A script is compiled when it is saved, like a rule: a step that does not
decode, an expression that does not compile, a wait longer than a run may
take, a field that makes no sense, all refused at save. You find out in the
editor, not at 3am with the pump half way through a wash.

## Fields are checked, never fixed

Before the first step runs, what the run was given is checked against the
fields: every value must be one its field takes, every required one must be
there, and a field the script does not have is an error rather than something
quietly ignored. **A value is never moved to fit.** 70 minutes on a field whose
maximum is 60 is refused, not trimmed to 60; `"12"` for a number is refused,
not parsed; 12.5 on a step of 5 is refused, not rounded. The value that goes on
to command equipment is exactly the one somebody entered, or nothing runs at
all. A refused run leaves no run behind: nothing started.

## Running one

| From | How | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| The Scripts screen | **Run** on its card, fill in the form | `scripts.run` |
| Its entity | **Run** on its tile, or `POST /api/services/script/turn_on` with the fields as the data | `scripts.run` |
| The API | `POST /api/scripts/{id}/run` with `{"fields": {...}, "reason": "..."}` | `scripts.run` |
| A rule | a `call_script` step | the rule's own |
| An agent | `run_script` over MCP | MCP writes on |

Operators run scripts. Admins write them. Running the CIP cycle is what the
button is for; deciding which valves the CIP cycle opens is an engineer's call
and it stays one.

A run answers as soon as it has started, with its id. Ask it to `wait` and it
answers when it ends, with its outcome and the trace of every step. **Stop**
(`POST /api/scripts/{id}/stop`, or `script.turn_off`) cancels every run of it
where it is, in every process, a wait or a delay included. Whatever a step had
already written stays written. Undoing is a write too, made without anybody
asking for it, to equipment that has already moved, and that is the
operator's decision, not ours.

## Every write goes through the gate

A script runs as **`script:<id>`**. Every write it makes, every service call,
every log line carries that as its actor, and every write is audited against
it in `GET /api/writes`, refused or not. The **source** is whoever started it:
`ui` from the screen, `automation` from a rule, `mcp` from an agent. That
matters because the gate decides on source. A script an agent starts writes as
`mcp`, and with `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_MCP_WRITES` off every one of its writes is
refused, exactly as the agent's own `write_tag` would be. `run_script` and an
agent's `script.turn_on` refuse up front in that case rather than running a
script whose every write is going to bounce.

The run records who asked (`actor`), how (`source`), and what called it
(`parent`: `automation_run:812`, `script_run:77`), so you can walk from a write
back to the rule, the script and the person or agent behind it.

## Ask first: the dry run

`POST /api/scripts/{id}/run?dry_run=true`, **Check first** in the run drawer,
or `run_script` with `dryRun`. The fields are checked the same way, then every
step is walked against the plant as it is right now:

- every `write_tag` and `call_service` is put to the write gate's own checks
  (`CheckWrite`, `Services.Check`), the same code the real write runs, so a
  dry run cannot say yes to something the real write would refuse for a reason
  the dry run did not check. Nothing is written, nothing is audited;
- a `condition` is evaluated now, and a false one ends the walk where it would
  end the run;
- a `set_variable` is bound, so the steps after it see what they would;
- a `call_script` walks the script it calls, its steps numbered under the call
  (`3.1`, `3.2`);
- a `wait`, a `delay`, and anything that writes to no equipment (a message,
  an HTTP call, an alarm raised) is `not_checked`. A dry run does not wait
  fifteen minutes to tell you what the tank will read then.

The first write that would be refused ends the walk, because it would end the
run, and the answer says so in the gate's words: `step 2 (call_service):
cip/pump: this tag is not marked writable`. A dry run that comes back clean is
advice, not a promise. A device can drop, somebody can disarm a tag, and a wait
gives the plant all the time it needs to change its mind between your check
and the step.

## Run modes

What a run asked for while another run of the same script is going does. The
same words a rule uses, with one difference.

| Mode | A second run |
|---|---|
| `skip` | refused, `409`, and a `skipped` run in the history saying why. **The default**, and the right answer for anything that commands equipment |
| `queue` | waits its turn, and starts when the one ahead of it has ended. One deep: a third is refused |
| `restart` | cancels the one in progress where it is, then starts once it has stopped. Two runs never overlap |
| `parallel` | runs alongside |

The difference: a rule's queue drops the older pending run in silence, and a
script's queue refuses the newer one out loud. A rule is fired by a trigger
that does not care. A script is asked for by somebody, or something, that may
be waiting on the answer, and "your run quietly never happened" is not an
answer.

A `call_script` step that waits for a busy script fails (`script busy`); one
that does not wait notes it in the trace and carries on, because all it was
ever going to do was start it.

`maxRuntimeSec` bounds one run, five minutes when it is zero. A run that runs
out of it is `timed_out`, whether it was between steps or in the middle of a
wait.

## Scripts calling scripts

A `call_script` step runs a script from a rule or from another script. With
`wait` the step takes the script's outcome as its own, and the script is part
of the run that called it: cancel the caller, or let it run out of time, and
the script it is waiting on stops too. Without `wait` the script is started
and left to finish on its own.

Two limits, both there because the alternative is a script that loops:

- **A script that would call itself is refused when it is saved**, directly or
  through any chain of other scripts: `script b would call itself: b calls a
  calls b`. The same goes for an edit that closes a loop.
- **Five deep, at run time.** A sixth script in one chain fails the step that
  would have called it, and the chain with it. And if a loop ever gets past the
  save (two processes saving two halves of it at the same moment), the run
  catches it: a script already running in its own chain is refused, not run a
  second time.

## Its entity

Every script is an entity, `script.<id>`, platform `script`. Its state is
`on` while a run of it is going, in any process, and `off` when none is; its
attributes carry its `mode`, how many runs are going (`current`), its
`fields`, and when it last started and how that ended. It is on the Entities
screen with a **Run** button, in `list_entities` over MCP, in `/api/states`,
and a rule can have a state trigger on it: "when the CIP cycle goes off, log
the batch". Deleting a script orphans its entity, the way deleting an alarm
definition does: an admin deletes the orphan when nothing refers to it any
more.

## The run history

Every run is a row in `script_runs`: who, how, the fields it was given after
they were checked, the trace of every step (resolved inputs, not templates),
how it ended and why. `GET /api/scripts/{id}/runs`, the run drawer, and the
[logbook](/iot/logbook/), where script runs are kind `script`, found by the
script's entity or by anything a run wrote to. The history keeps the newest
500 runs of each script, the same bound automation runs have.

A run's row is opened before its first step and finished after its last. The
process stopping cancels every run in progress where it is and records it as
`cancelled: interrupted by restart`. A run a crash cut off, with nobody left to
finish its row, is marked the same on the Gateway's next start. **Nothing
resumes a run.** Carrying on from step four of a CIP cycle an hour later,
unasked, against a plant that has moved on, is worse than saying it stopped.

## More than one process

The Gateway and an `--mcp-stdio` process beside it (or two pods mid-rollout)
both run scripts. A run's state lives in the database, and every process
listens for changes on `hotloop_script`, so:

- a script started in one process shows `on` in every process's entity;
- a script saved on one pod is the script on the other, and its runs there
  are cancelled if its steps changed;
- **Stop** stops every run of it, in every process.

A run mode is kept per process. Two processes can each start one run of a
`skip` script at the same instant. A plant running the same procedure from an
agent's helper process and the operator's screen in the same second has a
conversation to have that no lock of ours would settle.

## Backups

`scripts` and `script_runs` are in every backup and come back on a restore,
with the history. A run the backup caught in the middle comes back `running`
and is marked `interrupted by restart` on the first start, like any other.
See [BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/).

## The API

Every route, its permission and its answers are in [API.md](/iot/api/#scripts).

| Permission | viewer | operator | admin |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scripts.read`: list them, their runs | yes | yes | yes |
| `scripts.run`: run, dry run, stop, `script.turn_on`/`turn_off` | no | yes | yes |
| `scripts.write`: create, edit, delete | no | no | yes |
